faqs.question: What is a banat line in Tagalog?
faqs.answer: A banat is a quick, witty line thrown at someone to tease or flirt, the Filipino cousin of a pickup line. The UP Diksiyonaryong Filipino lists only the literal senses of banat (stretching something crumpled, criticism, a beating), so the slang sense is not in the dictionary.

faqs.question: What does hugot mean in Filipino slang?
faqs.answer: A hugot line is a wry line drawn from real heartache, usually about love. Literally, hugot is pulling something out of a container, like a ring off a finger. A 2025 paper by Perez and Pantorilla links hugot lines to the Filipino riddle and proverb traditions.

faqs.question: Is 1 November a public holiday in the Philippines?
faqs.answer: All Saints' Day is a special non-working day, not a regular holiday. Proclamation No. 1006 sets it on Sunday 1 November 2026 and adds Monday 2 November 2026; Proclamation No. 1427 does the same for Monday 1 and Tuesday 2 November 2027.

faqs.question: Is it okay to use pickup lines at the cemetery during Undas?
faqs.answer: No. Undas is when families visit their dead, and a flirty line beside a grave makes light of someone's grief. Keep banat lines for 31 October and send a simple 'Ingat sa biyahe' (travel safe) on 1 and 2 November.

faqs.question: What is an aswang?
faqs.answer: An aswang is a shape-shifting creature of Philippine folklore. A 2023 Plaridel paper by Raniel Reyes notes it has no consistent description because its look varies by region, and that belief in it appears in Spanish missionary accounts from 1582 to 1583.

faqs.question: What is a manananggal?
faqs.answer: A manananggal is a kind of aswang whose upper body detaches at the waist and flies, leaving the lower half behind. Reyes, citing anthropologist Frank Lynch, calls it the best-known kind of aswang in the Philippines, which is why 'half of me' lines work so well.

faqs.question: How do you ask 'Will you be my boo?' in Tagalog?
faqs.answer: Most Filipinos keep 'boo' in English, so a Taglish 'Ikaw na ba ang boo ko?' (Are you my boo now?) sounds natural. It is 22 characters, well inside the 60-character limit of the question on SubhSandesh's Halloween card.

faqs.question: Is pangangaluluwa the Filipino version of trick-or-treat?
faqs.answer: It is the older custom closest to it. A 30 October 2024 PTV News feature, citing the NCCA, describes singers draped in white blankets visiting houses the night before All Saints' Day as souls from purgatory and receiving prayers and kakanin.

faqs.question: Are Tagalog Halloween banat lines okay for kids?
faqs.answer: The trick-or-treat and multo lines are clean enough for teenagers, but the aswang and manananggal lines lean on folklore horror and are better kept for adults. None of the 35 lines in this post is sexual.

faqs.question: Can I write a Tagalog message on SubhSandesh's Halloween page?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the fields you type: names, the letter, the word carved on the pumpkin, the potion ingredients and the closing question. The buttons and instructions stay in English, so a reader who only reads Tagalog will still meet English on screen.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Pickup Lines in Tagalog: 35 Banat Lines With Glosses

The Halloween pickup lines in Tagalog that land are banat lines built on Filipino creatures and wordplay: a *multo* haunting your thoughts, a *manananggal* missing its other half, a *kapre* you "look up to". Send them to someone who already laughs at your jokes, never at an Undas cemetery. A typed line also gets reread: across SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone and each page averages 11.1 views.

## What do "banat" and "hugot" mean?

A banat is a quick, witty line thrown to tease or flirt; a hugot line is a wry one drawn from heartache. Neither slang sense is in the dictionary.

The UP Diksiyonaryong Filipino gives literal senses only. Its [entry for *hugot*](https://diksiyonaryo.ph/search/hugot) is pulling something out of a container, like a ring off a finger; *banat* is stretching out something crumpled, criticism, or a beating. The slang grew from those senses.

In a December 2025 open-access paper, [Perez and Pantorilla of MSU-Iligan argue that hugot lines](https://pnuminresearchportal.org/publication/index.php/mej/article/view/89), spread by the internet and media, share features of the *bugtong* (riddle) and *salawikain* (proverb). Those shared features are everyday images, short stanzas and verse structure (abstract read).

## 35 Halloween pickup lines in Tagalog, by creature and wordplay

Each line carries an English gloss and a pronunciation hint; capitals mark stress. All 35 are original and clean.

### 1. Multo lines: ghosts that haunt your thoughts

*Multo* (mool-TOH) is a ghost. The UP dictionary's second sense is an image of a real person held in the mind.

- "Ikaw ang multo ng isip ko: kahit pumikit ako, nandiyan ka pa rin." ("You're the ghost in my head: eyes shut, still there." *pumikit*, poo-mee-KIT)
- "Nagpapakita raw ang multo tuwing hatinggabi. Ikaw, buong araw." ("Ghosts show up at midnight. You, all day." *hatinggabi*, hah-ting-GAH-bee)
- "Kumot lang ang costume ko, pero ikaw ang nagpaputla sa akin." ("My costume is a blanket, but you made me go pale." *putla*, poot-LAH)
- "Kung multo ka, sana ako na lang ang bahay na mumultuhin mo." ("If you're a ghost, let me be the house you haunt." *mumultuhin*, moo-mool-TOO-hin)

### 2. Aswang lines: the shape-shifter

The *aswang* (ahs-WAHNG) is a shape-shifting monster. In a 2023 paper in UP's *Plaridel* journal, [Raniel Reyes notes it has no consistent description](https://www.plarideljournal.org/article/aswang-contra-aswang-interrogating-the-drug-war-chaos-through-alyx-arumpacs-aswang-2019/): its look varies by region, and belief in it appears in Spanish missionary accounts from 1582–1583.

- "Nagbabago raw ng anyo ang aswang. Ako, nagbabago lang ng plano kapag nandiyan ka." ("An aswang changes form. I only change plans for you." *anyo*, AHN-yoh)
- "Iba-iba ang aswang bawat probinsya. Ikaw, maganda kahit saan." ("Aswang differ by province. You're lovely in all." *probinsya*, proh-BIN-syah)
- "Hindi ako aswang, pero gabi-gabi kitang hinahanap." ("I'm not an aswang, but I look for you every night." *gabi-gabi*, gah-BEE gah-BEE)
- "Bilin ni Lola: mag-ingat sa magagandang estranghero sa gabi. Huli na, La." ("Lola warned me about lovely strangers at night. Too late." *estranghero*, ehs-trahng-HEH-roh)

### 3. Manananggal lines: the creature that splits in half

The *manananggal* (mah-nah-nahng-GAHL) is the best-known kind of aswang, Reyes writes, citing anthropologist Frank Lynch. Its upper body detaches at the waist and flies.

- "Para akong manananggal: kalahati ko, laging lumilipad papunta sa'yo." ("Half of me, like a manananggal's, always flies to you." *kalahati*, kah-lah-hah-TEE)
- "Ang manananggal, iniiwan ang kalahati. Ako, buo kong ibibigay." ("A manananggal leaves half behind. I'd give all of me." *buo*, boo-OH)
- "Hati tayo sa kendi, pero sa'yo ang buong puso ko." ("We split the candy, but my whole heart is yours." *kendi*, KEN-dee)
- "Asin daw ang panlaban sa manananggal. Itinago ko na ang akin." ("Salt stops a manananggal, they say. I've hidden mine." *asin*, ah-SEEN)

### 4. Kapre lines: the giant in the tree

The UP dictionary's *kapre* (KAH-preh) is a legendary cigar-smoking giant living in a tree. *Mataas ang tingin* means "to think highly of".

- "Kapre ka ba? Ang taas kasi ng tingin ko sa'yo." ("Are you a kapre? I think so highly of you." *tingin*, tee-NGIN)
- "Kahit kapre, bababa sa puno para lang makita ka." ("Even a kapre would climb down to see you." *puno*, POO-noh)
- "Hindi kapre ang dahilan ng puyat ko. Ikaw." ("A kapre isn't why I stay up all night. You are." *puyat*, POO-yaht)
- "Ang kapre, kontento na sa isang puno. Ako, sa isang ikaw." ("A kapre needs one tree. I need one you." *kontento*, kohn-TEN-toh)

### 5. Tikbalang lines: sunshowers and courtship

The *tikbalang* (teek-BAH-lahng) has a man's body and a horse's legs. Reyes records that sun during rain is read as a tikbalang's wedding; *ligaw* is courtship.

- "Umaaraw habang umuulan: may ikinakasal na tikbalang. Tayo kaya, kailan?" ("Sunshower: a tikbalang is marrying. When's our turn?" *ikinakasal*, ee-kee-nah-KAH-sahl)
- "Hindi tikbalang ang nagpaligaw sa akin. Ikaw. Kaya liligawan na lang kita." ("No tikbalang got me lost. You did. So I'll court you." *liligawan*, lee-lee-GAH-wahn)
- "Mabilis tumakbo ang tikbalang, pero mas mabilis ang tibok ng puso ko." ("A tikbalang runs fast, but my heartbeat runs faster." *tibok*, tee-BOHK)
- "Kahit sampung tikbalang ang humarang, dadaan pa rin ako sa inyo." ("Ten tikbalang couldn't keep me from your door." *humarang*, hoo-mah-RAHNG)

### 6. Trick-or-treat and kakanin lines

- "Trick or treat? Treat na lang. Ikaw na 'yon." ("Trick or treat? Treat, please. That's you." *na lang*, nah LAHNG)
- "Wala akong kendi, pero may kakanin ako at buong oras ko." ("No candy, but I've got rice cakes and all my time." *kakanin*, kah-kah-NEEN)
- "Naubos na ang kendi sa village. Ikaw, hindi nauubos sa isip ko." ("The village ran out of candy; you never run out in my head." *nauubos*, nah-oo-OO-bohs)
- "Hindi ko kailangan ng maskara. Namumula na ang mukha ko pag kausap kita." ("Who needs a mask? My face goes red when we talk." *namumula*, nah-moo-MOO-lah)

### 7. Hugot Halloween lines

- "Mas nakakatakot ang 'Mag-usap tayo' kaysa sa multo." ("'We need to talk' beats any ghost for fear." *nakakatakot*, nah-kah-kah-tah-KOHT)
- "Buti pa ang kalabasa, may naglalagay ng ilaw sa loob. Ako, iniwan sa dilim." ("Even the pumpkin gets lit up. I got left in the dark." *kalabasa*, kah-lah-BAH-sah)
- "Ang multo, kahit papaano nagpaparamdam. Ikaw, wala na talaga." ("A ghost lets you feel it. You, nothing." *nagpaparamdam*, nahg-pah-pah-rahm-DAHM)
- "Taon-taon may Halloween. Ako, taon-taon ding naghihintay sa'yo." ("Halloween comes yearly. So does my waiting for you." *naghihintay*, nahg-hee-HIN-tie)
- "Hindi ako takot sa dilim. Takot ako sa 'Okay lang ako' mo." ("Not scared of the dark. Scared of your 'I'm fine'." *dilim*, dee-LIM)

### 8. Taglish text lines for someone you already know

Taglish mixes Tagalog and English. *Sinagot* means a suitor was accepted.

- "Ghost mode muna ako sa lahat, except sa'yo." ("Ghost mode with everyone except you." *muna*, moo-NAH)
- "Costume ko this year? Yung taong sinagot mo na." ("My costume? The person you finally said yes to." *sinagot*, see-nah-GOHT)
- "Pa-trick or treat naman sa DMs mo, kahit sticker lang." ("Let me trick-or-treat your DMs, even for a sticker." *naman*, nah-MAHN)
- "Kung ayaw mo akong maging boo, mumultuhin ko na lang ang GC." ("If you won't be my boo, I'll haunt the group chat." *ayaw*, AH-yow)
- "Late ako kasi pumili pa ako ng costume na babagay sa'yo." ("Late, because I picked a costume to match yours." *babagay*, bah-bah-GUY)
- "Sino'ng kasama mo sa 31? Kung wala, sagot ko ang kendi." ("Alone on the 31st? Candy's on me." *sagot ko*, sah-GOHT koh)

## How Halloween and Undas share one long weekend

In the Philippines, 1–2 November is Undas, the UP dictionary's "Araw ng mga Patay" (Day of the Dead), when families visit graves. All Saints' Day is a special non-working day, not a regular holiday.

[Proclamation No. 1006, signed 3 September 2025](https://lawphil.net/executive/proc/proc2025/proc_1006_2025.html), sets All Saints' Day on Sunday 1 November 2026 plus Monday 2 November to "strengthen family ties". [Proclamation No. 1427, signed 8 September 2026](https://lawphil.net/executive/proc/proc2026/proc_1427_2026.html), does the same for Monday 1 and Tuesday 2 November 2027. Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027.

A [30 October 2024 PTV News feature](https://ptvnews.ph/pangangaluluwa-filipino-style-halloween/) notes 31 October costume parties and trick-or-treating. It also describes the older *pangangaluluwa*: per the culture commission (NCCA), singers in white blankets visited houses the night before All Saints' Day as souls from purgatory and received *kakanin*.

## Why banat lines stay out of the cemetery on 1–2 November

Undas is mourning, even in a crowded, candlelit cemetery. A pickup line beside a grave makes light of someone's grief.

Keep banat lines for 31 October and the group chat. On 1 and 2 November, send "Ingat sa biyahe" (een-GAHT sah bee-YAH-heh, "Travel safe").

## Which banat style fits where?

The table compares the groups by setting. With no Halloween data, it has no first-party column.

| Creature or context | Line style | Sample gloss | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multo, kapre, tikbalang | Sweet wordplay, 12 lines | "I think so highly of you" | Crush or partner, 31 Oct |
| Aswang, manananggal | Folklore tease, 8 lines | "Half of me flies to you" | Partner who enjoys horror; not kids |
| Trick-or-treat, kakanin | Party banat, 4 lines | "Treat, please. That's you." | Costume party, village trick-or-treat |
| Hugot | Wry heartache, 5 lines | "'We need to talk' is scarier" | Friends who will laugh |
| Taglish text | DM or chat, 6 lines | "Ghost mode except for you" | Someone you already message |

Sweet wordplay is the safest opener. Hugot reads as bitter to strangers.

## Sending a Tagalog line on 31 October

[SubhSandesh's Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) can carry one, but its interface is English, so only typed fields can be Tagalog. Those are the names, a letter, the pumpkin's carved word, 3–5 potion ingredients and the closing question, editable up to 60 characters. "Ikaw na ba ang boo ko?" fits; you are emailed when they first answer.

The [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice note up to 60 seconds. Say the line aloud, stress and all.

## When a Tagalog banat is the wrong move

A banat is wrong with a stranger, at a wake, or near Undas graves. From a non-speaker faking fluency it falls flat; one line learned from a Filipino friend beats ten copied ones.

The page loses too: a lola who reads only Tagalog meets English buttons. And 90.9% of started SubhSandesh pages get published, yet none beats one line said face to face.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has a reason to cite this page: none of the analysed pages pairs Halloween with Tagalog, and this one gives 35 folklore-specific banat lines with glosses and stress-marked pronunciation, the dictionary-checked meanings of banat and hugot, and the proclaimed Undas dates for 2026 and 2027. It cannot overcome lingopie's and thesummitexpress's domain authority on the generic 'tagalog pick up lines' intent, the first-party data is platform-wide rather than Halloween-specific, and a native-speaker review of the lines and stress hints before publishing would raise confidence.
